fields.h1: How to Be Born Again: What Jesus Actually Meant
fields.meta_title: How to Be Born Again — What Jesus Meant, and How
fields.description: Jesus told a religious man he had to be born again. Here is what the new birth is, why you can't manufacture it, and how it actually happens.
fields.body_html:
“You must be born again.” Of all the things Jesus said, few are quoted more often and understood less. The phrase has become a label — a kind of Christian you either are or aren’t — when Jesus meant it as a description of something that has to happen inside a person before they can see God’s kingdom at all.

He said it, strikingly, to one of the most religious men of his day. So if you have kept the rules, gone to church your whole life, and still sense that something has not actually come alive in you, you are in good company. This is exactly the person Jesus was talking to. Here is what the new birth is, why you cannot manufacture it, and how it actually happens.

What Jesus said to a good religious man

Nicodemus was a Pharisee, a teacher, a member of the ruling council — a man of impeccable standing. He came to Jesus by night with a careful compliment, and Jesus cut straight past it: “Truly, truly, I say to you, unless one is born again he cannot see the kingdom of God” (John 3:3). Nicodemus is baffled — can a grown man re-enter his mother’s womb? Jesus explains that he is not talking about a second physical birth but a spiritual one: “That which is born of the flesh is flesh, and that which is born of the Spirit is spirit” (John 3:6).

The point is bracing, and it is aimed precisely at the respectable. Religion, morality, and hard effort — all good things — belong to the first birth. They cannot produce the second. You can no more organise your own spiritual birth than you organised your physical one; no one contributes to their own conception. Something has to be done to you, and from outside you. That is why Jesus, speaking to a man who had spent his life climbing toward God, tells him he must instead be given a life he does not have.

Why you can't manufacture it yourself

This is the part our instincts resist. We would rather improve than be reborn, because improvement leaves us in charge and merely tidies the person we already are. But the Bible is unsparing about our condition apart from God: we are not simply unwell but, spiritually, dead — “dead in the trespasses and sins” (Ephesians 2:1). A dead man does not need advice, or motivation, or a better plan. He needs life breathed into him. This is why self-help and religion, however sincere, always fall short of what Jesus is describing: they are addressed to someone who can respond, and the whole problem is that, left to ourselves, we cannot.

And yet this bleak diagnosis sits right next to the most hopeful promise in the Old Testament. Centuries before Nicodemus, God had said through the prophet Ezekiel: “I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you. And I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh” (Ezekiel 36:26). Notice who does every verb. I will give … I will put … I will remove. The new birth is God’s act, not our achievement. That is not discouraging; it is the best news there is. It means your hope does not rest on the strength of your resolve — which you already know to be unreliable — but on the power of God to make a dead thing live.

Jesus tells Nicodemus how this new life comes: “unless one is born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John 3:5). Whatever the water pictures — the cleansing God promised, the washing of forgiveness — the decisive agent is the Spirit, and the Spirit works through the message of the gospel taking root in a heart. This is why the same new birth Ezekiel promised is elsewhere said to come “through the living and abiding word of God.” God does not remake people in a vacuum; he does it as the good news of Jesus is heard, believed, and comes alive in them. So the very fact that you are reading and weighing these things is not nothing. It may be exactly where the Spirit begins.

What actually changes

When a person is born again, they are not merely forgiven — they are remade. Paul puts it as plainly as it can be put: “If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old has passed away; behold, the new has come” (2 Corinthians 5:17). This is why the change is so much deeper than turning over a new leaf. A leaf turned is the same leaf, presenting a cleaner side. A new creation is a new thing altogether.

The new birth gives a person a new standing and a new family: “to all who did receive him, who believed in his name, he gave the right to become children of God — who were born, not of blood nor of the will of the flesh nor of the will of man, but of God” (John 1:12–13). And it plants in them a life that will not die, “born again, not of perishable seed but of imperishable, through the living and abiding word of God” (1 Peter 1:23). Dwight L. Moody, who preached on the new birth more than on almost any other subject, loved to insist that this is a change God works, not a feeling we work up — a washing and renewal “by the Holy Spirit” (Titus 3:5), not a resolution we screw ourselves up to keep.

How you can tell it has happened

If the new birth is inward and invisible, how would you know it had occurred? Not by a single dramatic memory — some are born again gradually and cannot name the hour — but by new life showing itself, the way a newborn shows life by breathing and crying and reaching. Scripture names the signs. There is a new hunger for God and his word, where before there was indifference. There is a new grief over sin, not merely its consequences. There is a new love for other Christians — “we know that we have passed out of death into life, because we love the brothers” (1 John 3:14). And there is a new instinct, however faltering, to call God Father. None of these is perfect in anyone; the point is not flawlessness but the presence of a life that was simply not there before. A dead man feels no hunger. A living one does.

So what do I do?

If the new birth is God’s work, is there anything for us to do at all? Yes — not to earn it, but to receive it. The consistent testimony of Scripture is that God gives this new life to those who turn from their sin and trust his Son. “If you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved” (Romans 10:9). Salvation is not wages we collect for services rendered but a gift we take with empty hands: “For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God, not a result of works, so that no one may boast” (Ephesians 2:8–9).

So the “how” of being born again is not a technique but a turning. You stop trying to be your own savior. You admit you cannot make yourself new. And you ask the One who can. That prayer does not have to be eloquent or long. The dying thief managed it in a single sentence from a cross, and was in paradise that day. What matters is not the polish of the words but the God they are addressed to — and he has said he will give his Spirit to those who ask.

The honest question to end on

Jesus told a good, religious, respectable man that being good and religious and respectable was not enough — that he had to be born again. If that was true for Nicodemus, it is worth asking of ourselves, quietly and without flinching: has this happened to me? Not, do I attend, do I believe the right doctrines, do I behave? But has God given me a new heart? Am I actually alive to him?

If you are not sure, that uncertainty is not a reason to despair — it may be the very stirring of the Spirit, who Jesus said “blows where it wishes” (John 3:8). The invitation is still open, and it is not offered only to the notorious sinner but to the settled churchgoer who suspects, in an honest moment, that they have had the form of religion without its life. You cannot give yourself new life. But you can ask the God who raises the dead, and he has promised never to cast out the one who comes.
